# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major source of morbidity and mortality despite substantial advances in pharmacological and device-based therapy. Although there has been remarkable progress in the treatment of HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), morbidity and mortality are still substantial. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) benefits patients with a prolonged QRS duration, but roughly two-thirds of patients with HF do not meet CRT criteria, leaving an important therapeutic gap [1]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) was developed to address this unmet need. Cardiac contractility modulation signals are nonexcitatory electrical signals delivered during the cardiac absolute refractory period that enhance the strength of cardiac muscular contraction.

## Mechanisms of action

CCM delivers high-amplitude biphasic impulses to the interventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, so that contractility is augmented without triggering an additional action potential. These high-amplitude, biphasic impulses seem to alter intracellular calcium handling, resulting in an increase in myocardial contractility without an associated increase in oxygen consumption; the left ventricular pressure–volume loop is shifted to the left. The energetic neutrality of this inotropy was demonstrated in failing canine hearts, where enhanced inotropic state of the failing left ventricle by cardiac contractility modulation electrical signals is not associated with increased myocardial oxygen consumption [2]. Beyond acute effects, chronic CCM appears to drive favorable molecular remodeling. In dogs with chronic HF, long-term CCM therapy improves LV systolic function, with reversal of global, structural, and biochemical remodeling [3]. CCM signals also normalize phosphorylation of key proteins and expression of genes coding for proteins involved in regulation of calcium cycling and contraction, and in human myocardium cardiac contractility modulation electric signals induce reverse molecular remodeling, including downregulation of fetal/stretch genes and upregulation of calcium-cycling genes [4,5]. A contemporary synthesis notes that CCM may attenuate and in some cases reverse many of these changes by improving Ca2+ handling and metabolic efficiency, reversing the fetal gene program, reducing interstitial fibrosis, and increasing phosphorylation of titin [6,7].

## Clinical trial evidence

The first chronic human experience demonstrated mid-term safety and efficacy in patients with systolic HF [8]. The first randomized, double-blind, double-crossover trial (FIX-HF-4) enrolled 164 subjects with ejection fraction below 35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms who received a CCM pulse generator; peak VO₂ and quality of life worsened when CCM was switched off and improved when switched on, supporting a treatment effect [9]. The larger FIX-HF-5 trial randomized 428 NYHA class III or IV patients with ejection fraction ≤45% to CCM plus optimal medical therapy versus optimal medical therapy alone; the study met its primary safety end point, but did not reach its primary efficacy end point, a responders analysis of changes in ventilatory anaerobic threshold [10,11]. However, in a prespecified subgroup analysis, significant improvements in primary and secondary end points were observed in patients with ejection fractions ranging from 25% to 45%.

This subgroup hypothesis was tested prospectively in FIX-HF-5C. A total of 160 patients with NYHA functional class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration <130 ms, and ejection fraction ≥25% and ≤45% were randomized to continued medical therapy or CCM for 24 weeks. The difference in peak VO₂ between groups was 0.84 ml O2/kg/min, satisfying the primary endpoint. The composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization at 24 weeks was also significantly reduced (10.8% vs 2.9%, p = 0.048), findings that supported FDA approval [12,13]. A simplified two-lead system was then evaluated in FIX-HF-5C2, in which patients experienced the same or even greater clinical effects than in the prior FIX-HF-5C study while the number of device-related complications was reduced [14].

## Meta-analyses and registry data

Pooled analyses have generally confirmed functional benefit while highlighting limited mortality data. An individual-patient-data meta-analysis found that CCM significantly improved peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, and quality of life measured by the MLWHFQ [15]. An updated meta-analysis of randomized trials included four RCTs with 801 patients, with a mean ejection fraction of about 29% and a mean QRS duration of approximately 106 ms [16], while an earlier analysis cautioned that CCM did not significantly improve all-cause mortality or all-cause hospitalizations [17,18]. Real-world data from the prospective CCM-REG registry of 503 patients from 51 European centres reported that CCM improved functional status, quality of life and LVEF, reduced HF hospitalization rates, and survival at 1 and 3 years was significantly better than predicted by the MAGGIC risk score [19]. A single-arm meta-analysis similarly observed reverse remodeling, with LVEF increasing by a mean of 5.96% [20].

## Patient selection, guidelines, and future directions

CCM has been positioned for symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who are not CRT candidates, and it is suggested for consideration by the European Society of Cardiology guidelines in patients with symptomatic HF on optimal therapy with normal or mildly prolonged QRS duration and reduced EF [21,22,23]. Evidence suggests CCM is particularly beneficial in patients with baseline EF between 35% and 45% [24,25]. Regulatory labeling has broadened applicability, since recent FDA labeling specifically removed the requirement for normal sinus rhythm, so CCM can be offered to patients with HFrEF who are in atrial fibrillation [26,27]. Interest is expanding toward HF with preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction, where mechanistic work has shown that CCM signals improve exercise intolerance and maladaptive regulation of cardiac key proteins for systolic and diastolic function in HFpEF [28,29]. The ongoing AIM-HIGHer program and next-generation devices combining CCM with defibrillator functionality are anticipated to clarify the role of this therapy across the HF spectrum [30].

## Conclusion

CCM is an established device option that improves exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life in carefully selected patients with HFrEF and narrow QRS, with growing registry evidence of reverse remodeling and reduced hospitalization. Adequately powered, blinded outcome trials—particularly in HFmrEF/HFpEF and in defining mortality effects—remain the principal evidence gaps.
